segments.text: All right. Well, good afternoon, and welcome, everyone. Are we live?
Yes.
Yep. Excellent. All right. Well, welcome to the Social Services and Community
Select Committee. And we are again hearing submissions this afternoon on the
Disability Support Services Bill.
I might do a quick
go around the table, just on who's here.
So I'm Joseph Mooney, the member of Parliament, South Island, and the chair of the
committee.
And my name is Laura McClure. I'm a the ACT Party member based
in Christchurch.
Kia ora koutou. Priyanka Radha Krishan, Labor list Member of Parliament based
in the Maungakiekie electorate and disability issues spokesperson.
Great. Thank you. Well, welcome. Our first submitter this afternoon
is Ms. Joanne Marshall in person.
Welcome.
We're
fortunate to have the support of the New Zealand Sign Language
interpreter with us in person here today as well.
Well, welcome. We have five minutes with you when you're ready.
Fire away when ready to go.
I'm sorry.
I'm sorry.
10 minutes.
Oh, sorry. Sorry, 10. Yes. No, you're right.
So kia ora, afternoon all.
My name is Joanne.
I appear before you as an author of comprehensive written submission currently
before this House as an intersectional deaf analysis
managing progressive, highly volatile neurological reality
to oppose this bill in its current form.
I know this committee has sat through wads of repetitive submissions.
You have heard sectors' collective pain, and you have heard our
anger over the rushed 25-day timeline.
I'm not here to repeat those grievances.
I'm here to provide this room with an objective, macro-level
dissection of the asymmetric risk-shifting
exercise disguised as public policy within this text.
Clause 7
framed disability support strictly through the lens of available
funding.
This represents an ideological inversion of New Zealand's
legacy of leadership.
Rights do not emerge because a treasury forecast says they are affordable.
Rights exist because we are human.
The absolute role of primary legislation is to safeguard
personhood, not to create transparent conveyor belt for
erosion.
When statutes leave core human protections out of primary text,
public systems do not become efficient.
They become abusive. I have physical evidence
of such friction here with me today, which is a letter from the Rotorua
Lakes Hospital ED management.
In the middle of an acute medical crisis, management actively
weaponized rigid commercial procurement contracts to deny
my preferred interpreters, NZSL interpreters,
denying access to language itself.
They prioritized system convenience over my statutory right to safe,
informed consent.
I hit the same institutional wall within the criminal justice
system, navigating a five-year process involving police,
government agencies, 10 lawyer teams, and four
judges, which concluded in every single arbitrary charge
being completely dismissed. When
disability support shifted to MSD from the
House, funding for interpreters in legal settings was quietly
terminated without community consultation.
The majority of Deaf New Zealanders are being forced to advocate for
language access through friction-heavy health and legal
processes, judged by hearing officials who possess
zero linguistic and cultural awareness.
This isn't efficiency. It's systematic
fragmentation of justice.
The government's primary defense of Clause 8 is that
it merely reflects current practice regarding family support.
This is a profound legal illusion.
This is an unbridgeable constitutional gulf between an
operational assessor gently acknowledging existing family goodwill
and a primary statute explicitly codifying family liability
in the first instance.
The moment you write those words into law, you transform supportive
relationship into legal barrier to entry.
You move benchmark from wrapping care around a citizen to calculating
how much unpaid labor you can legally extract from a private family
unit before the state is forced to intervene.
This assumption of empty family capacity assumes baseline of
help that does not exist.
Within my own family unit, we concurrently navigate
deafness, complex neurological fluctuations,
traumatic brain injury, post-concussion syndrome, borderline
personality disorder, alongside narcolepsy with cataplexy.
We are already operating at 100% capacity.
When you tip state liabilities into a unit that is already full,
you do not build resilience.
You engineer structural household collapse.
We have been told by government members that centralizing power under Clauses
10 and 11 creates transparent framework that
constrains the minister.
This is a fundamental misreading of administrative law.
Transparency without accountability is just an open view of an
empty safety net
Currently, when a minister alters settings by historic cabinet memo,
they operate in a vulnerable grey area, which is legal grey
area, challengeable in the High Court as ultra vires.
The bill fixes that legal vulnerability for state.
It hands the minister a bulletproof statutory shield, making
future funding cuts legally unchallengeable and completely
insulated from judicial review.
If this constellation government genuinely
possesses good intentions, let us test them today.
Establish an unalterable legislative firewall within the primary
text of this bill.
Use primary statutory anchors to explicitly state that no ministerial
program or secondary regulation can ever
legally supersede the New Zealand Sign Language Act 2006,
the Bill of Rights Act 1990, the Human Rights Act
Te Tiriti,
or our international obligations under Articles 43,
21, and 28 of the UNCRPD.
If you write that firewall into statute, you protect community.
If you refuse, you confirm that this bill is
designed to allow future ministers to turn off our fundamental rights
behind closed doors.
My Deaf community and my disability sector's personhood is a
protected right,
not an administrative variable.
Thank you, and I welcome questions, if any.
Thank you. Very good.
Thank you.
Just one quick clarification, and I think you might have touched on
this towards the end of your
oral submission.
In your recommendations, recommendation seven, you've said that
any replacement legislation contain clear statutory
protections
against arbitrary reductions. Just wanted to clarify whether you were
referring to more detail in primary leg or writing
in the requirement for consultation in secondary leg,
or both?
Personally, I'm speaking for my voice and my experience and history-
Yeah
... of what I have lived.
Yeah.
That would have to be something actually consulted because we all have different
perspectives.
Okay.
We're not all the same. So what I say will be different from
what somebody else says.
So it's best to actually do the consultation through all the
deaf and disability sector and ask everyone on that one.
Okay.
Yeah.
Joanne, a question about section eight, and you've probably
heard, or you may and may not have heard me ask some
submitters before. But the section eight says
that family support,
in the first instance, where appropriate.
I'm wondering if you have any comment for the committee about that language.
I was waiting for that question.
Sure.
Because you've asked many.
Yes.
I have lived that already. I don't have to wait to see.
I understand it because MSD has been doing that to me already.
All my own
funds, I don't have KiwiSaver anymore. It's gone.
I've had to fund my own equipment, like a bed.
I've had to fund wheelchair hire when I need it because, as I
said, I can wake up and I can't walk. I can wake up blind.
My condition is complex on top of being deaf.
So for me, it's not a wait and see.
I can speak saying
my family's already doing it. My son moved in with me five years
ago. We combine resources, but even then, we're still having
to advocate for our rights within MSD now.
We're still having to use those protections.
We have to educate, we have to teach, because the knowledge isn't there by
the frontline staff.
And even then, I fought against going against the supported
living on it for many years. I'm on it because of doctor
orders and because of having to be arbitrarily
placed before the justice system without any evidence.
So I have fought that.
So I come with a different story and background,
and I stand here today because of me fighting my rights,
and using those protections.
So it's not an easy thing to do. I've been tired.
I've nearly locked it, closing down,
but if I do, then who else will?
So I'm kind of leading the charge on issues that haven't even been
experienced yet.
So I welcome the consultation and discussions
because I come with that. Nobody can take that from me.
Well, thank you very much, and thank you for coming and making a submission to the
committee this afternoon. Appreciate it.
Thank you.
You're
welcome.

Elliot Yates in person.
Elliot, welcome.
Hello, everyone.
We have 10 minutes with you this afternoon. The time is yours when you're ready.
Yeah. Hello, everyone. My name is Elliot,
and my last name is Yates.
I'm a university student at present, and also deaf
and also a wheelchair user. I have quite an independent life,
and I have lots of support, which I do need to carry out my
life
I've also been to another university previously, and I graduated
from that university.
I did struggle with having supports in university, and
I have struggled with accessing other supports in my life as well to
now.
And I think I'm not alone. I think lots of other disabled people are in the
same sort of situation.
Some people don't have any supports, and that's quite a struggle,
and I can feel a victim of the system sometimes.
I sort of feel that we're being told what to do in this
space
in regards to disability support issues.
And I feel that the government is making up excuses and sort
of sidelining us in respect to this bill.
There's lots of paperwork,
and I feel that
is a lot of stress as well, and we've given everything,
in regards to paperwork, and it's just too much.
Too much of a demand for us going through life, and I don't think that's good being
told what to do.
Also, with carer support
and family support,
I think that's really not their
job to take on those extra responsibilities.
And that successful ruling was made
in regards to these services, and I do think that
when that went through the Supreme Court, there was a lot of work done in
that respect.
And the government is sort of, again, what I feel is not very interested
and just sort of
pushing us to the side and relying on family or
spouses to pay up for things that we need or to cover our
care, and I feel that there's no respect there from the government.
I'd like to live a normal life working and income and
supporting society.
Also,
with all these other issues,
and not just me alone, other disabled people,
having family there to support and look after
people such as myself and others, that is quite
disappointing. It also opens the doors to abuse
that is not seen because it's happening within that family
environment, where if there's more professional supports, maybe less abuse
would happen.
And I just feel that because of those reasons, the bill is not fair.
And I feel that the government is not doing a great job at
supporting us. They're not thinking about us.
And this has been a historic problem.
If one could live independently with all the right supports
around them, they could live a very good and lovely
independent life.
And I do worry about this shift that's coming from
one being independent and being able to control their own lives to one
being more under the DSS system and being told what to
do.
And I feel that there's no consultation with us as disabled
people and the control is taken out of our hands.
And
to organize all the supports,
we also
feel that
we're being sidelined. There's funding cuts, there's
been changes to the law at a level that we're not involved in.
And I feel now
that it's just sort of the wheels in process, and everything is
getting done automatically with this bill, and we're not being
consulted. The power is being sort of taken from us.
We're being dictated to about what we should be doing.
So nobody is listening to us, and I
therefore do not recommend accepting this bill.
I hope it gets thrown out of government.
And for us, as disabled people, trying to
navigate the system
can be very tricky.
And we are New Zealand citizens. We are able to
get involved in elections and partners with support.
We're equal members. We should be equal members of society.
But this bill should take into consideration the
UNCRPD,
the recommendations there. It should be following that, and it also
should be thinking about human rights.
So with this submission, I really want you to understand the damage
that if this bill did get passed through Parliament, the damage it would cause.
And again, I think it ignores us as disabled
people,
and it's not taking us into consideration.
We're losing out on funding supports.
We're not being
involved or being able to participate, and I think
the bill also needs to consider Te
Whānau Ora as well and the principles there.
And if this bill does get passed, it will make it very difficult for
disabled people,
and also difficult for disabled Māori people as well.
And it'll make our future even harder than it is now.
And I think it'll affect all people all over New Zealand.
So just keep in mind that you're working together with all of us,
not without us. We want to be involved
in this.
I'll save my blessing and love with you. Thank you.
Thank you. Um, Priya.
Um, thank you. You've said throughout your
presentation, which was very good by the way, um, that
you don't want to be told-
Well, I'm glad it's over too.
I can see that. Um, that you don't want to be told what to
do, that from your perspective, disability communities are co- constantly
being sidelined, you're worried about funding cuts and you've mentioned
consultation as well. Um,
are you referring to consultation prior to this bill
being introduced to the House or are you talking about
the ministerial program, so the, um, secondary
legislation that the minister can design which doesn't
require consultation with disability communities,
or both?
That's meaning like
if changes can be made to the bill-
Mm
... I think there would be a better pathway to go forward.
So I'm just thinking about the future.
If this bill gets passed, there's obviously going to be implications.
It will affect us as disabled people, it will affect funding.
So yeah, I would like it to be scrapped
and changes made to it.
And just in terms of-
Yeah, I really think it should be-
I, I just have a question, Priya
... thrown into the rubbish bin.
Yep.
If the bill is passed.
Oh, okay.
Um, Elliot, Elliot, um, in, in your submission, um, you
said that, uh, there are funding cuts.
I'm just wondering for you to explain what you mean because the, this government
has invested the most ever into disability support services with almost $3 billion
a year.
I'm more worried about the future-
... possibility of funding cuts.
Mm.
Like if life is going to be different,
uh, whether it's National, Act, New Zealand First, whichever party,
I don't know. But just wondering about the impacts
going forward.
Because I want a good bill, a strong bill, that
can't be adapted going forward. So I want it there to protect
us.
Mm.
You know, and if we need something as disabled people,
we should be able to access that.
And I know with funding, definitely helps us as
disabled community to go forward.
But if funding gets cut by the government,
then I think that the risky sort of
situation, we need a bit of, uh, power and safety there in
regards to the bill.
Mm.
Is that the moment, the way the bill's written? I really don't like that.
I, I wish it, it was pushed to the side and a new
bill was created. Thank you.
All right. Well, um, thank you very much, Elliot, for coming and making submissions
to the committee this afternoon and sharing your perspective.
Thank you.
Thank you.
All right, our next submitter, uh, submitters are, are Deaf Aotearoa New Zealand,
um, via Zoom.
Um, good afternoon and welcome. We have, uh, 10 minutes with you this afternoon.
The time is your- yours when you are ready.
Thank you. Tena koutou katoa. Thank you for the opportunity to speak.
Uh, my name is Lachlan Keating. I'm the Chief Executive of Deaf Aotearoa.
Hang on a second. Um, think this is how we were instructed.
Sorry, can you just, uh, just to let Lara know, they're just moving your screen, so
we can't see you.
Um, you want the template then.
Um, I need to be able to see-
Yeah, sorry. I was too early.
It's all good.
Is that all good there?
Yep.
It works?
Yep.
There we go.
All good.
Tena koutou. My name is Lara Draper.
Uh, I am General Manager for Adults and Senior Services at Deaf
Aotearoa.
Back to Lachlan.
Okay. So Deaf Aotearoa, we're a national organization representing the voice of and
providing services to several thousand Deaf people,
including Turi Māori. I just want to acknowledge both Joanne and
Elliot who spoke before us and shared their lived experience, who have both made
very powerful presentations and submissions this afternoon.
So just as a bit of background, we were established in 1977 to advocate for
specific services to be established for Deaf people and for qualified New
Zealand Sign Language interpreters be trained and supported so that Deaf people can
have the same access to health services, information,
government agencies, and daily life as hearing people
Now, as an advocacy and a service provider, these are two roles we generally keep
separate, but are also roles that complement each other.
Being a service provider means that we see firsthand the barriers deaf people
face every day.
This knowledge means we're able to advocate strongly and quickly for these barriers
to be removed and can use real-life examples to support our advocacy
work.
There are many examples of where our service provision has informed our advocacy,
which has then directly improved outcomes for deaf people.
Under our DSS contract, Deaf Aotearoa provides NASC, DIAS, hearing
assistive technology, and NZSL interpreting services.
Our DSS-funded services do not cover all the needs of deaf people, and a
major current issue is that the types of meetings where interpreters were
previously funded by DSS has now changed.
This means that deaf people are now missing out on interpreters for key parts of
everyday life, such as meetings with lawyers and accountants,
buying or renting a house, going to the vet, some mental health
services, and so on.
We support having a clear framework for Disability Support Services.
However, we oppose the bill in its current form.
We want to acknowledge the work undertaken since the March 2024 changes
and the effort to clarify the criteria around DSS funding, as a
system of multiple funding streams was confusing, inconsistent, and
unfair.
However, there remains too many gray areas, and Lara will now speak to
those.
Thank you.
So the bill, it looks like it's steering towards a situation
where responsibility for care rests on family and
whanau.
So this is a real issue for family, that family first model, where
deaf people are expected to rely and depend on family
and whanau in the first instance before then
accessing the funded services and supports.
For deaf people, that can be an issue of safety,
and it affects deaf people in
that we would need to rely on family members, and it actually takes away the rights
of deaf people, our right to autonomy, self-determination, choice,
and control. It gets taken away.
For our community of deaf people, including turimāori,
this bill, as it stands, is really in opposition to
the New Zealand Sign Language Strategy 2025,
launched
by Minister Louise Upston.
The strategy itself recognizes that
relying on family members
to use them as interpreters is harmful.
It states that relying on children of deaf adults, CODAs
is what we call them,
they should not be used as interpreters at all.
Deaf people should not have to rely on family members or
friends, and in particular their own children, to interpret for
them. For example, in medical situations, government
services, or anywhere else where any other social and
cultural
events. Access to qualified interpreters is absolutely
critical in order to provide equity,
independence, and cultural safety and participation in society.
This bill suggests that
access is really that family first model.
So it does actually talk about using CODAs or family members as a first port of
call for those supports before accessing those funded sign
language interpreters.
So the bill and the NZSL strategy there are odds with one another.
So why this is a problem is that there's the assumption that
all families out there who have deaf members and hearing members
within them are all fluent in New Zealand Sign Language.
That's simply not the case.
There are many families out there who just can't sign.
So that means that there are a lot of deaf people who are very isolated
in their own homes.
So replacing professional interpreters
in favor of using a family member is not acceptable.
It's a real failure to provide equity of
access and safe and independent
communication, and is a breach of privacy and informed consent as
well.
Also, placing that responsibility on family members, and especially on
children, is onerous and for deaf family members is not
safe. It's a breach of the Convention on the Rights of Persons
with Disability, Article 21B and E,
and also the Health and Disability Commission Code of Rights, in
particular right number five,
stating that the provision of qualified interpreters is imperative
in order to ensure that there is that equal access for deaf people.
Another issue that I want to raise is that of
workforce development. There's a real gap there.
So the bill,
it doesn't recognize that gap. I understand that the bill
is setting up legislative framework
for Disability Support Services, absolutely.
However, it doesn't speak to
the workforce itself and the continuation, the
sustainability of that workforce.
Strengthening it. For example, how people can access
training and development in a funded way,
and accessing high-quality DSS services.
For deaf people, for access, they rely on NZSL
interpreters who are qualified and professional.
It also needs deaf and hearing staff who are fluent in NZSL.
So the workforce is already under pressure at the moment and underfunded.
And it's a real issue.
So this bill is assuming that the supports are already there, but in reality
there's just not enough. There are not enough interpreters.
There are very few trilingual interpreters who are proficient in all three
languages of English, Te Reo, NZSL.
So the workforce development is an absolutely critical area, and without
that, and without funding to support that, interpreters and deaf leaders and
professionals, the system absolutely can't deliver equitable access
or culturally appropriate support for deaf people.
Without targeted funding,
really focused on training pathways to
support deaf people to actually come into the workforce themselves to
become professionals, and also, get into
leadership roles and those actually delivering the services.
Really, this bill doesn't speak to that, and it's actually providing more barriers
and reducing access for deaf people.
Deaf people have been advocating in this space for
decades, and it's now time for action.
This is really important because policies after policy after policy of
advocating from deaf people, communicating and there's all
these decisions being made,
but these decisions are being made without us about things that are impacting our
everyday lives.
So the bill is really not recognizing deaf people
within it.
The disability support services are really-- They're not a
discretionary benefit. They're actually fundamental to
our access to equal participation in society.
Thank you, and over to you for any questions.
No. Thank you, Lachlan and Lara. I might have a quick question
actually for you, Lara. Just I'm wondering which part
of the bill made you think that
families would have to provide sign language interpreting services and
particularly children, because I don't see that actually in the bill
myself.
It's not in the bill,
but it's implied.
It's implied.
So it's not clear. It doesn't say that it's not appropriate.
Where it talks about it's appropriate to use family members, you can
take from that, that they could be used as interpreters.
Currently, deaf people don't actually have access to interpreters in many settings
or just to participate in society and everyday life. There's a real gap there.
Again, thank you, Lara and Lachlan, for your submissions this afternoon, for your
written submission as well.
Thank you.
Mm-hmm.
All right. Thank you both. Appreciate it.
Thank you.
Our next submitter is the Office of the Ombudsman in person.
Well, good
afternoon and welcome.
Kia ora tātou. Thank you for the opportunity to speak with you briefly
today on what is an important piece of legislation.
The context in which we are here
is that the Office of the Ombudsman is an independent monitoring
mechanism,
monitoring the state
on its performance against the UN Convention on the Rights of
People with Disabilities,
and the rights and protections of those people
within our community.
In that context,
the explanatory general policy statement, which talks about a new
foundational legislative framework to strengthen, stabilize, and
provide disability
support services by improving consistency, fairness, and
transparency
is something that we can all support.
And which, in fact, has been advocated for
by this community for many, many years.
Unfortunately, key parts of the proposed
bill
do not reflect
that ambition and in our view will not
sustain that ambition. And the
first specific thing that I would refer to in that
context, and you'll have seen it in our submission,
is that the bill makes no reference at all to
the UN convention.
If you're going to establish a framework for long-term
sustainability, for equity, for fairness, for
transparency,
then to ignore the provisions of the UN convention to which New
Zealand is a signatory, to make no explicit reference
to those convention provisions and key parts of the bill, and I've
instanced clauses eight, 10, and 11
in the written submission.
And to effectively
marginalize the foundational
principles of that legislation in the construct of the
bill,
creates, in our view,
real problems.
And you see it
in the next specific provision that I want to talk
to, which is the one that Lara has just
addressed in some detail,
which is the emphasis which is being placed
in this bill and in this legislation on the
responsibilities of whānau and family, and the
extremely broad definition of whānau and
family which is
proposed by the legislation.
Now, as you know, the UN convention is primarily aimed
at enabling adult people with disability
to lead their own lives on their own terms,
in their own way.
And this provision
potentially reduces their capacity and
autonomy to do that.
It reduces it because many whanau are not
in a position to provide the sort of support the government
expects from them.
It reduces it because it creates responsibilities and
potentially tensions within a whanau and within a
community
that can be
translated onto the person
who has the disability.
They're seen as being responsible for the tensions and difficulties or
challenges that are being faced within that particular
whanau.
And it creates tension as well
between this desire of individual adult
people with disability to be able to live their own lives,
and the ability to fund that and get the
appropriate support for living that life
in the way that is contemplated by the bill.
So we only have a brief time. We could have talked about other elements of the
legislation, and no doubt, I hope we'll have an opportunity to do that.
I'm here with members of the disability rights team from our
office who are actively engaged in
this work day by day by day.
And our strong
recommendation to this committee is that you
think carefully about the inclusion of the
provisions or reference to the provisions of the convention in the
legislation, as we've referenced and instanced in our submission.
Other countries are doing that and do do that, and it
provides you then with a much stronger foundation for the
ambition that you're expressing for this legislation.
And then think carefully about the responsibilities that you're imposing on
whanau and family, because you may actually drive
adverse outcomes that limit the lives of
people with disabilities, when that, I suspect, is not the
intention.
Thank you very much for making a submission this afternoon.
Thank you for your written submission as well.
Thank you.
The next submitter is TalkLink Trust and Person.
Good afternoon, welcome.
All right, so we have five minutes with you this afternoon.
The time is yours when you're ready.
Kia ora. Tena koutou katoa, and thank you for the opportunity to speak.
My name is Wayne Ferguson, and I'm the Chief Executive of TalkLink Trust,
and with me today... Roseanna Tilyard, speech and language therapist and
team lead in the Wellington area.
So for over 30 years, TalkLink has supported disabled
people across Aotearoa to communicate, participate, and
live independently through assistive and communication
technology.
TalkLink is a nationwide service that covers all ages,
so we have a unique bird's eye perspective of disability
services and the need across New Zealand.
Today, I acknowledge the significant effort and mobilization of the
disabled community, their whanau and organizations who have
deeply engaged with this process, often under pressure and
within tight timeframes. That reflects just how important
this bill is.
I'm aware that many others have highlighted the areas of the bill that need
urgent attention and change.
We have specific points to raise and believe this is an
incredible opportunity to make significant positive
change.
So we are here representing not only our organization,
TalkLink, as a service provider, but also many New Zealand
people who literally do not have a voice without
assistive technology. For them, this bill determines
whether they are heard or not.
What changes would we like to see? Our core position is that
this bill should be paused and redesigned through genuine
co-design, and our contribution is specific.
Communication must sit at the center of the system and should be
part of standard infrastructure and not just an add-on.
We are asking for three changes. Firstly, commit to genuine
co-design with disabled people, whanau, and providers.
Partner early, build trust, and use the available frameworks.
Just as the previous speaker has said, UNCRPD to treat New
Zealand Disability Strategy to guide the process.
These frameworks are there and exist.
Second, we would like to see funding sustainability addressed
directly. This bill reflects constraint and
shifting responsibilities but does not resolve longstanding
underfunding nor provide a sustainable pathway
forward.
From what I've heard so far in these submissions, disabled
people and their wider communities understand the
realities of affordability, budget boundaries,
and solid financial guardianship.
And thirdly and critically, we ask that assistive technology,
especially communication assistive technology, is recognized and
included as core infrastructure and not
as optional supports.
Because without communication, this bill risks entrenching a system
where disabled people are still not fully heard.
In particular, people cannot participate in decisions, they can't
access services safely, and they cannot exercise choice or
control.
So our solutions, we do see this as a once in a lifetime
opportunity to reset the system properly.
Our solutions are clear and practical.
We would like to see investment earlier, particularly in assistive
technology. In our work every day, we see
people who have the right communication tools.
